extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, news editors, and writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing news reports using the inverted pyramid: present the most important facts first (lead), then follow with information in descending order of importance so readers can leave at any point and editors can cut from the bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise most important information at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: The widest part at the top represents the most substantial, interesting, and important information that the writer means to convey, illustrating that this kind of material should head the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the article like an upside-down triangle: put the key facts and most newsworthy material in the opening sentences so readers encounter them first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the five Ws (and how) in the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Who, when, where, why, what, and how are addressed in the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the lead so it answers the essential questions; the article's example (Lincoln assassination coverage) shows routine placement of these elements in the opening. A more pyramid-conscious writer might move additional critical details into the first two sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not bury the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite, the failure to mention the most important, interesting or attention-grabbing elements of a story in the opening paragraphs, is called burying the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the most newsworthy/attention-grabbing facts appear in the opening paragraphs rather than being delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise material in descending order of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The tapering lower portion illustrates that other material should follow in order of diminishing importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the lead, present supporting details and background in decreasing priority so readers who stop reading still have the essentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Summary news lead" / Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid is sometimes called a summary news lead style, or bottom line up front (BLUF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise summary lead that gives the bottom line immediately; this is the institutionalised form of placing the most important material first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an optional hook or prologue
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid may also include a 'hook' as a kind of prologue, typically a provocative quote, question, or image, to entice the reader into committing to reading the full story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hook can precede or accompany the inverted-pyramid lead to draw readers in, but it should not obscure the core facts of the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make stories easy to edit by 'cutting from the bottom'
rubrics_metrics.description: This system also means that information less vital to the reader's understanding comes later in the story, where it is easier to edit out for space or other reasons. This is called 'cutting from the bottom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange less essential details toward the end so editors can shorten copy by removing trailing paragraphs without losing key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with a kicker (when appropriate, e.g., feature pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than petering out, a story may end with a 'kicker'—a conclusion, perhaps call to action—which comes after the pyramid. This is particularly common in feature style articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For feature or narrative-leaning pieces, consider adding a concluding 'kicker' after the descending-information structure to provide closure or a call to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense material when necessary (telegraphic/concise reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention of the telegraph sparked its development by encouraging reporters to condense material, to reduce costs, or to hedge against the unreliability of the telegraph network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constraints demand brevity (technical limits, cost, or transmission reliability), compress reporting to prioritise the essentials in the lead and remove peripheral detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt the inverted pyramid to other formats and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a common method for writing news stories and has wide adaptability to other kinds of texts, such as blogs, editorial columns and marketing factsheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same prioritisation principle (important first, details later) across different media and formats, adapting tone and level of background detail to the audience and medium.
